excerpt: A childhood dream of Baguio, a shared geography in Laguna, and an American internee’s World War II memory intersect to reveal how places hold on to us long after we leave them.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
bodyText:
"We leave something of ourselves behind when we leave a place, we stay there, even though we go away. And there are things in us that we can find again only by going back there." — Pascal Mercier, *Night Train to Lisbon*

There is a simple comfort in finding common ground with a stranger. If Pascal Mercier was right when he wrote that we leave bits of ourselves in the places we depart, then geography serves as a silent ledger of where we have been.Growing up poor, I spent years longing for Baguio City, the so-called City of Pines, tucked cool and misty into the Cordillera Mountains. My cousins went there when we were children, and I envied them bitterly. Years passed before I finally set foot on its mountain roads, brought there by a university job arranging workshops for textbook writers.Beyond fulfilling a childhood wish, I had simply wanted to know what it felt like to live in a place where the air turned crisp, and Baguio offered that relief. All of which brought me, eventually, to Katherine Ream Sobeck.

![](/assets/uploads/cms/katie-ream-sobeck-bw-.jpeg "A black and white illustration of Katherine Ream Sobeck based on a photograph posted by her daughter Eileen Sobeck on Instagram.")

Though her family lived in San Pablo for only a few short years before moving north, I counted the Reams as *kababayan*. As a teenager, I used to travel to San Pablo every month for meetings of the *Kapisanan ng Agham ng Lunduyang Timog Katagalugan*, representing Laguna as its public information officer. That small overlap of earth was enough to build a bridge, and it made me eager to read her account of the war years.

When she sat down decades later to record her oral history, thousands of miles from her birthplace, her memory remained astonishingly clear. Where psychology tells us the mind usually buries painful events to shelter the consciousness from terror, Katherine’s memory worked with the exactness of a surgeon. She knew the layout of her past precisely—where to look, where to stop, and what to lay bare.

She remembered the morning of December 7th down to the smallest detail. It was her twelfth birthday, and her father was driving her and her siblings to school when news arrived that Pearl Harbor had been attacked. In the sudden confusion of leaving the classroom, she left a sandwich untouched on her desk, a small loss that lingered in her mind for years. For a twelve-year-old girl, the war did not begin with grand speeches or distant maps; it began with an unfinished lunch and the sudden end of a normal morning.

As I read through her transcript, what struck me was not just the hardship of internment, but how people managed to build a workable life behind barbed wire. Katherine’s father was a resourceful man who ran the camp’s makeshift electrical shop. He turned trash and scraps into things the community needed—hammering copper tea kettles out of old fire extinguishers, shaping umbrella ribs into knitting needles, and fixing broken spoons and forks. When his own lower dental plate broke, he gathered scrap aluminum, melted it down, and cast a new set himself. It worked, though as Katherine noted, aluminum conducts heat remarkably well, giving him a sharp shock the first time he took a sip of hot coffee. That home-made dental plate now rests in the National Dental Museum in Baltimore, a durable little monument to a man's refusal to give up.

Katherine remembered the camp’s officers not as abstractions, but as distinct human beings. There were civilian commandants like Nakamura, the carpenter, and Suda, the photographer. She remembered Commandant Tomibe, who protected the internees by covertly dropping word before high-ranking Japanese inspections so the prisoners would not look too well-fed or cheerful, preserving their meager rice rations.

And there were moments of plain human decency. One evening, a young mother could not pacify her colicky baby. A Japanese sentry carrying a rifle with a fixed bayonet walked up and asked to take the infant. The mother hesitated,fearing the worst, but the sentry simply placed the baby over his shoulder and walked his post with him for his entire shift. He returned the next night and did the same thing until the child fell asleep, giving the entire barracks a full night of rest.



After Christmas in 1944, as mountain supplies ran low, the Baguio internees were moved south to Bilibid Prison in Manila. It was a miserable place—the cots were alive with bedbugs and the rice was full of worms. Yet outside the walls, the war was coming to a swift conclusion. General MacArthur had landed at Leyte in October, and American forces were moving quickly across Lingayen Gulf by January. Katherine realized later that moving to Manila had saved them from being caught in the destructive crossfire that eventually leveled Baguio. American units, including the 1st Cavalry, were pushing hard toward the capital to reach the camps before the guards could carry out standing orders for mass executions. Relief reached Santo Tomas on February 3, 1945, and Bilibid the following day.

Through Katherine’s eyes, Baguio was never just a point on a military map or a scenic hill station. It was a place where people baked pie crusts out of cold cream, put on amateur performances of *Our Town*, consulted a makeshift Ouija board for news, and kept their dignity intact.

Reading her interview, I felt that familiar, honest sense of connection. Separated by time and circumstance, we were nevertheless tied to the same soil, the same pine air, and the same mountain city that marks everyone who spends time within it. Mercier was right after all: we leave a part of ourselves behind in the places we hold dear, and sometimes,years later, we find those lost pieces waiting for us in the plain lines of an archive, alive and unaltered.
